claim: Tim Miller uses only 5 workflow folders (FINVA); argues folders force exclusivity that hurts as projects grow.
quote: A file either is in a folder, or it isn't. You can't have a file that exists in two folders at the same time… As your project grows and changes, folders have a hard time keeping up.

claim: Steph Ango (Obsidian CEO) uses ~4 folders and organises via links/properties; navigates with Quick Switcher and backlinks, not the file tree.
quote: I avoid folders because many of my entries belong to more than one area of thought.

claim: Recommends shallow folders + MOCs + tags as discovery signals; tags are signals not structure; cap nesting at ~2 levels.
quote: Tags are signals, not structure—use them for discovery, not primary organization.

claim: Official Obsidian docs define backlinks pane with Linked Mentions and Unlinked Mentions sections.
quote: Unlinked mentions are backlinks to any unlinked occurrence of the name of the active note.

claim: MOCs and tags are complementary not opposing; MOCs are curated frozen state, tags qualify status.
quote: MOC's and tags are for me 2 ways to look at / for content. They are complementary instead of opposing themselves.

claim: Forum users argue MOCs allow description/ordering/formatting that tags can't; recommend starting with tags and adding MOCs only when needed.
quote: MoC lets you describe the document you are linking to, and also order and format the documents in a manner appropriate to the work at hand.

claim: MOCs are 'folders on steroids' — a note can appear in multiple MOCs unlike folders; types include basic, contextual, and meta-MOCs.
quote: MoCs work as 'folders on steroids,' allowing multiple organizational structures for the same note—unlike traditional folders that limit notes to single locations.

claim: Nick Milo's ACE = Atlas, Calendar, Efforts; based on STIR model; Relatedness is handled via links not folders.
quote: The 'STI' of STIR can map to the ACE folder structure—and in the process give us a universal folder system that optimizes for recall!

claim: LYT framework popularised MOCs; community testimony of going folderless then re-adding a few folders for balance.
quote: Learning first to get rid of a rigid folder-based system was scary but useful. And later, bringing back some folders finding a balance between the structure and flexibility was a big deal.

claim: System for linking 500 orphan notes: one wikilink per new note, Graph View to spot orphans, 3 MOCs to absorb them, #needs-link weekly batch.
quote: Start with just three MoC notes covering your broadest topics. Every new note you create should have at least one [[wikilink]] before you close it.

claim: Official Obsidian: linking notes is the platform's core power; non-existent links appear muted, acting as future seeds.
quote: The true power of Obsidian lies in being able to link your notes together.

claim: Five-level MOC adoption progression: isolated notes → linking → first MOC (Dump/Lump/Jump) → MOC-of-MOCs → Home note. 'Think and link first.'
quote: Don't start by perfecting your organizational system. Think and link first and organize later once the need becomes obvious.

claim: Strategic title selection makes unlinked mentions surface free connections; works as low-maintenance retrieval layer.
quote: Create note titles that match the text you expect to appear naturally in your writing. Use these titles for recurring categories such as journals, fitness logs, stock symbols, or project names.

claim: PARA (Projects, Areas, Resources, Archives) — Tiago Forte's cross-tool method, frequently used as an Obsidian scaffold.
quote: Tiago Forte's PARA Method... Projects, Areas, Resources, Archives.

claim: Recommends against strict PARA in Obsidian; argues folder exclusivity fights graph structure; selective borrowing only.
quote: Forcing traditional folder structure is limiting the benefits of that system and creating unnecessary effort in maintenance by moving files from folder to folder.

claim: Cautions against 'creating for the graph' — writing pointless notes or forcing links just to see new dots.
quote: Creating for the graph rather than for yourself can lead to writing short, pointless notes just to see a new dot appear, or forcing links between ideas that didn't really belong together.

claim: Avoid circular backlinks (A→B, B→A with no semantic value) as a backlink antipattern.
quote: Be careful not to create circular backlinks (i.e., Note A links to Note B, and Note B links back to Note A). This can create confusion and make it difficult to navigate your notes.
